newsitem.title: USA: Jewell lawyers deny report of waning FBI interest.
newsitem.headline: Jewell lawyers deny report of waning FBI interest.

text.p: Attorneys for U.S. Olympic bomb suspect Richard Jewell on Tuesday denied a newspaper report that FBI interest in the ex-security guard has begun to wane.

The Atlanta Journal-Constitution on Tuesday quoted Jewell's criminal attorney, Jack Martin, as saying FBI investigators had suspended surveillance outside his 33-year-old client's home and were becoming less interested in Jewell as a suspect.

He also said the FBI was returning "most of the property" seized from Jewell during searches of his suburban Atlanta apartment, a rural cabin where he once lived and a shed in north Georgia, according to the newspaper.

Jewell was working as a security guard near Centennial Olympic Park in downtown Atlanta when a bomb exploded during a free concert on July 27, leaving two dead and wounding more than 100 people. He later became the only named suspect in the investigation but has never been charged with any crime.
Martin was unavailable for comment on the newspaper report. But Lin Wood, another Jewell attorney, responded to a Reuter query on Martin's behalf by saying the report was untrue.

"Richard Jewell remains a suspect. Nothing's changed. There has been a change from the public surveillance to what they describe, in the U.S. attorney's office, as a less obtrusive surveillance," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"The U.S. Attorney's office has indicated to us that it's only a change in form. They have not indicated that it has reflected a lessening in any way of interest in Mr. Jewell."
Last month, Jewell's four-member legal team was allowed to see sealed FBI documents that were expected to shed light on the government's grounds for suspicion against their client.

His attorneys, who say they may sue the FBI and the news media for ruining Jewell's name, also have begun making their client available for press interviews. On Tuesday, they showed no interest in allowing media interest in the case to wane.

Wood acknowledged Jewell recently turned down a new request for an FBI polygraph test. But he accused the FBI of leaking a "false report" that federal officials offered to free Jewell from suspicion if he had passed the test.
Both the FBI and the U.S. Attorney's Office in Atlanta declined to comment on the case.

Until last week, a team of FBI agents had spent more than two months following Jewell's every movement, by staking out his suburban Atlanta apartment and using several chase cars to trail him while on the road.
